newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugoslav dinar extends mystery black market fall.
newsitem.headline: Yugoslav dinar extends mystery black market fall.

text.p: Yugoslavia's dinar continued its black market slide on Tuesday, losing a further 7.5 percent to stand at 4.3 to the German mark, street dealers said.
They expected the dinar to retain its downward trend.
"Nobody seems to know what's going on. The (street) market is suddenly flooded with dinars, and we will certainly not sell marks," one dealer told Reuters.
The dinar's dive began over the long New Year and Orthodox Christmas holidays. Banks and firms will reopen on January 8. Before the holidays the dinar stood at 3.8 to the mark.
Analysts and bankers say it is not the banking system which is flooding the market, shaking what seemed the only stable pillar of the country's fragile monetary system during 1996.
"Accounts of the Yugoslav banks stood around 64 million dinars in the red on December 31. Even the banking giants such as Beobanka and Vojvodjanska were insolvent," one private banker said.
"Banks are no longer market makers as they used to be during the 1993 hyperinflation."
In 1993, when daily inflation was 60 percent, banks flooded the street market with worthless dinars, obtaining hard currency cheaply from citizens.

Economists put the dinar's real value at around five or even 5.5 to the mark, but said a dinar devaluation would not be efficient for the economy, which is barred from key international financial institutions.
"A devaluation would bring a few benefits, but overall it is not desirable at the moment," said Branislav Pelevic of the Belgrade School of Economics.
Economists said the underlying problem was mistrust of the country's entire economic and monetary system.
"Today, nobody believes the current official dinar rate is sustainable, and confidence is what counts in economic policy," Miroljub Labus of the Economics Institute said.

Yugoslavia's government and central bank vowed late last year to keep the dinar stable at 3.3 to the mark in 1997. It was fixed at 3.3 after a 70 percent devaluation in November 1995. Until then it had been fixed to the mark at par.
